case.dispatchHook: Geology alert near Tallahassee! Broken rock and moved rock got filed as the same thing.
briefing: Agent, a road crew near Tallahassee logged eight rock changes along a creek bank.
Their report calls every single change erosion, but the engineers need the real facts!
Sort what broke the rock from what carried it away, then check the minerals and resources in the file.
Take your time with the clues, Agent. Let's get the creek bank data back on track!

lab.intro: The road crew jumbled its field notes! Sort whether each clue broke rock in place or carried pieces away.

bins.name: Weathering
bins.hint: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, and the broken pieces stay right where they are.

bins.name: Erosion
bins.hint: Erosion carries pieces of rock and soil from one place to a new location.

cards.name: Live oak root
card: A root grows into a crack in a boulder.
The crack gets wider and the rock splits.
cards.why: The oak root broke the rock apart right where it sat, so this is weathering!

cards.name: Frozen crack
card: Water fills a crack in a mountain rock.
It freezes, takes up more space, and splits the rock.
cards.why: Freezing water expanded and split the rock in place, so this is weathering!

cards.name: Hot days, cold nights
card: Desert rock heats up by day and cools at night.
Over many years, thin pieces flake off.
cards.why: Heating and cooling cracked pieces off the rock without moving them, so this is weathering!

cards.name: Blowing sand
card: Wind blasts sand grains against a rock tower.
The face of the rock wears into tiny bits.
cards.why: Blowing sand chipped the rock into smaller bits where it stood, so this is weathering!

cards.name: Creek after a storm
card: Brown water rushes down the creek.
It carries sand and pebbles downstream.
cards.why: Rushing creek water carried sand and pebbles downstream, so this is erosion!

cards.name: Rockslide
card: Loose rocks tumble down a steep hill.
They end up in a pile at the bottom.
cards.why: Gravity pulled the rocks down the hill to a brand-new spot, so this is erosion!

cards.name: Glacier
card: A huge sheet of ice slides slowly downhill.
It drags rocks and soil along with it.
cards.why: Slow-moving ice dragged rocks and soil to a different place, so this is erosion!

cards.name: Moving dune
card: Wind blows sand from one side of a dune to the other.
The dune slowly shifts across the beach.
cards.why: Blowing wind carried sand to a new spot across the beach, so this is erosion!

case.debriefClosed: Awesome job, Agent! The creek bank report is fixed, and every rock clue is filed where it belongs.
case.debriefOpen: This case stays open for now, Agent. Keep your streak plate handy and come back soon to help the quarry crew!

items.stem: Agent Maya spots a pink granite boulder in her field kit. Deep underground, melted rock cools slowly and turns solid to form granite. Which rock type is granite?
why: Spot on! Igneous rock forms when hot melted rock cools and hardens.
Sedimentary rock forms from pressed and cemented layers of sand and mud.
Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure.
Fossil rock is not one of Earth's three main rock categories.
items.alt: Three rock samples: a layered rock, a middle sample labeled Granite, and a banded rock.
items.tisCheck: Three rock categories by formation (SC.4.E.6.1); granite as igneous; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Igneous confused with metamorphic; inventing new rock categories.

items.stem: Agent Leo inspects the fort walls at Castillo de San Marcos in St. Augustine. The walls are made of coquina, which contains broken shells pressed together in layers. Which kind of rock is coquina?
why: Igneous rock forms from cooling lava or magma, not pressed shells.
Spot on! Sedimentary rock forms when layers of shells and sand press together.
Metamorphic rock forms when intense heat and squeezing bake older rock.
Volcanic rock is another name for igneous rock that cools from lava.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the layered rock on the left labeled Coquina.
items.tisCheck: Coquina as sedimentary rock; Florida history context (Castillo de San Marcos); no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Rocks with shells thought to be metamorphic or volcanic.

items.stem: Agent Sam examines a rock sample. Deep inside Earth, high heat and pressure squeeze solid rock until its mineral grains line up in wavy bands to form gneiss. Which type of rock is gneiss?
why: Igneous rock forms from melted rock that cools and hardens.
Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sand and shells pressed together.
Spot on! Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure squeeze older rock into wavy bands.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of pressed shells and skeletons.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the banded rock on the right labeled Gneiss.
items.tisCheck: Gneiss as metamorphic rock; formation by heat and pressure; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Wavy bands confused with sedimentary layers.

items.stem: Obsidian is a black, glassy igneous rock found near volcanoes. How does an igneous rock like obsidian form?
options: From layers of dead sea plants pressed together.
From great heat and pressure changing limestone.
From sand grains cemented together over time.
From melted rock that cools and turns solid.
why: Pressed plant material forms coal, which is sedimentary.
Heat and pressure changing rock creates a metamorphic rock.
Cemented sand grains form sandstone, a sedimentary rock.
Obsidian is an igneous rock formed when melted rock cools quickly.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the dark glassy rock in the middle labeled Obsidian.
items.tisCheck: Obsidian as an igneous rock formed from cooling melted rock; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Glassy rocks thought to be man-made; cooling confused with heating.

items.stem: Much of Florida sits on a thick layer of limestone. Long ago, tiny sea organisms died and settled to the ocean bottom, forming layers that hardened into rock. Which statement best classifies Florida limestone?
options: It is sedimentary because it formed from layers of shell and skeleton pieces.
It is igneous because it formed from melted rock deep underground.
It is metamorphic because it was melted completely into hot lava.
It is a mineral because all rocks in Florida are made of a single crystal.
why: Limestone is sedimentary because it forms from layers of bits of sea life pressed together.
Igneous rocks form from melted rock, not from sea organism remains.
Complete melting forms magma or lava, which cools into igneous rock.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of minerals, not a single mineral.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the layered rock on the left labeled Limestone.
items.tisCheck: Limestone classification in Florida context; sedimentary formation; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Limestone thought to be igneous; confusion between rocks and minerals.

items.stem: Agent Maya studies a rock sample that contains fossil imprints of ancient fern leaves. In which group of rocks are fossils usually found?
why: Extreme heat from molten magma destroys living things and their shapes.
Spot on! Sedimentary rocks bury plants and shells in soft mud where fossils form.
Intense heat and squeezing crush or destroy fossils inside metamorphic rock.
Volcanic rocks form from scorching lava that burns fossils away.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the layered rock on the left labeled Rock with fossil.
items.tisCheck: Fossils found in sedimentary rock; content limit: no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Belief that fossils survive molten lava or intense heat.

items.stem: Agent Rosa compares three rock samples in a table. Sample X cooled from melted rock inside Earth. Sample Y formed from pressed layers of river sand. Sample Z changed under high heat and pressure. Which statement correctly matches each sample to its rock category?
options: Sample X is sedimentary, Sample Y is igneous, and Sample Z is metamorphic.
Sample X is metamorphic, Sample Y is sedimentary, and Sample Z is igneous.
Sample X is igneous, Sample Y is sedimentary, and Sample Z is metamorphic.
Sample X is igneous, Sample Y is metamorphic, and Sample Z is sedimentary.
why: Sample X cooled from melted rock, which makes it igneous rather than sedimentary.
Sample X cooled from melted rock, so it cannot be metamorphic.
Spot on! Cooled melted rock is igneous, pressed sand is sedimentary, and baked rock is metamorphic.
Sample Y formed from pressed sand layers, so it is sedimentary rather than metamorphic.
items.alt: A table showing three rock samples and how each sample formed.
items.tisCheck: Matching three rock categories to formation processes; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Swapping sedimentary and metamorphic formation; confusing melted rock with heat and pressure.

items.stem: Students observe a sample of granite with large, visible mineral grains. The teacher explains that granite is an igneous rock. How did this rock form?
options: Layers of clay were dried by the Sun.
Shell pieces were pressed together in seawater.
Solid rock was bent without melting.
Melted rock cooled and turned into solid rock.
why: Drying clay forms mudstone, which is a sedimentary process.
Pressing shell pieces forms sedimentary rocks like coquina or limestone.
Bending without melting describes metamorphic rock formation.
All igneous rocks, including granite, form when melted rock cools and hardens.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the middle rock sample labeled Granite.
items.tisCheck: Granite as an igneous rock formed from cooled melted rock; no mineral composition of rocks; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Sunlight drying rocks confused with igneous cooling.

items.stem: Scientists group rocks into three main categories based on how they formed. What are the three main categories of rocks?
why: The three major groups of rocks classified by formation are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.
Hard, soft, and rough describe texture and hardness, not rock formation groups.
Minerals and fossils are materials found in rocks, not the three rock categories.
Grain sizes describe texture rather than the three main rock categories.
items.alt: Three rock samples: a layered rock, a glassy rock with holes, and a rock with folded bands.
items.tisCheck: Three rock categories by formation (SC.4.E.6.1); no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Grouping rocks by texture or physical feel instead of formation.

items.stem: A hiker finds a rock near a Florida spring that shows flat layers of pressed sand and shell bits. Which statement explains why this rock is sedimentary?
options: It cooled quickly from boiling red lava.
It formed when pieces of sediment piled up and cemented together.
It melted completely deep under Earth's crust.
It changed shape only from hot underground steam.
why: Cooling lava forms igneous rock, not layered sedimentary rock.
Sedimentary rocks form when sediments collect in layers and become cemented together.
Completely melting rock produces melted rock that hardens into igneous rock.
Heat and pressure changes produce metamorphic rocks.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the layered rock on the left labeled Spring rock.
items.tisCheck: Sedimentary formation in Florida spring setting; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Sedimentary layers confused with lava flows.

items.stem: During mountain building, buried rock is squeezed by high heat and pressure until it changes into slate. Which category of rock is slate?
why: Igneous rock forms from melted rock that cools and hardens.
Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sediment, not from high heat and pressure.
Rock changed by high heat and pressure without melting is metamorphic.
Fossil rock is not one of the three main categories of rocks.
items.alt: Three rock samples, with the banded rock on the right labeled Slate.
items.tisCheck: Metamorphic formation by heat and pressure; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Believing rock changed by heat must have melted into igneous rock.

items.stem: A student creates a table to sort four rock descriptions into rock categories. Which entry in the table represents an igneous rock?
options: Description 1: layers of crushed clam shells cemented into stone.
Description 2: solid rock changed by high heat and deep pressure.
Description 3: mud layers pressed flat over thousands of years.
Description 4: melted rock that cooled slowly inside Earth.
why: Crushed shells cemented together form sedimentary rock.
Solid rock changed by heat and pressure is metamorphic rock.
Pressed mud layers form sedimentary rock.
Melted rock that cools and hardens inside Earth forms igneous rock.
items.alt: A table describing four rock formation methods.
items.tisCheck: Sorting rock descriptions by category; igneous defined by cooling melted rock; no rock cycle.
items.misconceptions: Metamorphic rock formed by heat and pressure confused with igneous rock.

items.stem: Agent Ava rubs a mineral across a rough white tile. It leaves a line of colored powder. Which property is Ava testing?
why: Luster describes how shiny or dull a mineral's surface looks in light.
Spot on! Streak is the color of the powdered mark left on a tile.
Hardness measures how easily a mineral can scratch another object.
Cleavage describes how a mineral splits smoothly along flat surfaces.
items.alt: A mineral sample dragged across a white tile, leaving a colored line, with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Mineral properties only; only the seven allowed minerals; no hardness scale; no identifying a mineral from its properties.
items.misconceptions: Streak confused with luster or with hardness.

items.stem: Agent Leo tries to scratch two minerals with a steel nail. The nail scratches calcite. The nail does not scratch quartz. What does this test show?
options: Quartz and calcite have the same luster.
The nail is harder than both minerals.
why: Check the scratch test! The softer mineral is the one that gets scratched.
A scratch test compares hardness, not how shiny a mineral looks.
The nail could not scratch quartz, so the nail is softer than quartz.
Spot on! The steel nail scratched calcite but not quartz, so quartz is harder.
items.alt: A table: the steel nail scratched calcite but did not scratch quartz.
items.tisCheck: Hardness compared with a scratch test; only the seven allowed minerals; no hardness scale; no identifying a mineral from its properties; no numbers.
items.misconceptions: The scratched mineral thought to be the harder one; hardness confused with luster.

items.stem: Agent Sam tests a sample of pyrite that looks shiny and gold. When it is rubbed on a white tile, it leaves a greenish black streak. Why do scientists often test streak and not only look at color?
options: The outside color of a sample can change, but the streak color stays the same.
Streak shows how hard a mineral is.
Color is always the best way to tell minerals apart.
Streak shows how much a mineral weighs.
why: Spot on! Outside colors can change or fool you, but a mineral's streak stays the same.
Hardness is tested with a scratch test, not by color powder.
Different minerals often share the same outer color, so color alone can fool you.
A balance measures mass, while rubbing on a tile tests streak.
items.alt: A gold-colored mineral dragged across a white tile, leaving a greenish black line, with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Color and streak as properties, using pyrite as a named example the student does not identify; only the seven allowed minerals; no hardness scale; no identifying a mineral from its properties.
items.misconceptions: Color thought to be the most reliable property; streak confused with hardness or with mass.

items.stem: A student finds three rocks. Rock 1 has layers with bits of shell in it. Rock 2 is glassy with tiny holes. Rock 3 has bands that look squeezed and folded. Which statement tells how each rock most likely formed?
options: Rock 1 formed from cooled melted rock, Rock 2 from heat and pressure, and Rock 3 from pressed layers.
All three rocks formed from cooled melted rock.
Rock 1 formed from pressed layers of sediment, Rock 2 from cooled melted rock, and Rock 3 from heat and pressure.
Rock 1 formed from heat and pressure, Rock 2 from pressed layers, and Rock 3 from cooled melted rock.
why: Layers with shells come from sediment, not from melted rock.
Only the glassy rock with holes shows signs of cooled melted rock.
Layers with shells mean sedimentary, glassy with holes means igneous, and squeezed bands mean metamorphic.
Folded bands come from heat and pressure, and the glassy rock came from cooled melted rock.
items.alt: Three rock samples: a layered rock, a glassy rock with holes, and a rock with folded bands.
items.tisCheck: Three rock types by how they formed (SC.4.E.6.1); no changes from one rock type to another; no mineral makeup of rocks.
items.misconceptions: Rock types mixed up; all rocks thought to come from lava.

items.stem: Over a very long time, layers of sand and shells pile up on the floor of the Gulf. The layers are pressed together and cemented into rock. Which type of rock forms this way?
why: Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools.
Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change a rock that already exists.
Sedimentary rock forms from layers of sediment, like sand and shells, pressed and cemented together.
A mineral is one of the materials that make up rocks, not a type of rock.
items.alt: Three rock samples labeled A, B, and C: a layered rock, a glassy rock with holes, and a rock with folded bands.
items.tisCheck: Rock type by how it formed, in a Florida limestone context; no changes from one rock type to another.
items.misconceptions: Rocks and minerals treated as the same; any pressing linked only to metamorphic rock.

items.stem: A student breaks open a rock and looks at it with a hand lens. She sees grains of different colors and shapes. Which statement about rocks and minerals is true?
options: Rocks are made of one or more minerals.
Minerals are made of many kinds of rocks.
Every rock is made of only one mineral.
Rocks and minerals are exactly the same thing.
why: The grains she sees are minerals, and rocks are made of one or more minerals.
This is backward, since minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
The different grains show that a rock can hold more than one mineral.
A rock is made of minerals, so the two are not the same thing.
items.alt: Five lab tools on a bench with the hand lens labeled.
items.tisCheck: The role of minerals in forming rocks; no mineral makeup of any named rock; no mineral identified.
items.misconceptions: Rocks and minerals reversed or treated as the same thing.

items.stem: Agent Maya tries to scratch four minerals with a fingernail. The fingernail easily scratches talc, but it does not scratch quartz, feldspar, or pyrite. What does this test show about these minerals?
options: Talc is the softest of the four minerals.
Talc is the hardest of the four minerals.
All four minerals have the same streak color.
A fingernail is harder than quartz and pyrite.
why: Spot on! The fingernail scratched only talc, proving talc is the softest mineral here.
A mineral that gets scratched is softer, not harder, than the rest.
Scratching a mineral tests its hardness, not its streak powder color.
The fingernail could not scratch quartz or pyrite, so it is softer than both.
items.alt: A table shows that a fingernail scratched talc but did not scratch quartz, feldspar, or pyrite.
items.tisCheck: Hardness compared with a fingernail scratch test on talc, quartz, feldspar, and pyrite; allowed minerals only; no Mohs scale numbers; no identifying an unknown mineral.
items.misconceptions: The scratched mineral thought to be the harder one; hardness confused with streak.

items.stem: Most white sand on Florida Gulf beaches is made of tiny, clear grains of quartz. When a scientist rubs a quartz grain against a glass plate, the quartz scratches the glass. What property of quartz does this test show?
why: Luster describes the way light bounces off a mineral surface.
Scratching another object tests how hard a mineral is to scratch, which is hardness.
Streak is tested by rubbing a mineral on a white tile to see the color of its powder.
Cleavage describes how a mineral splits along flat surfaces.
items.alt: A quartz grain rubbed across a glass plate, leaving a scratch, with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Quartz hardness tested against glass; Florida beach sand context; allowed minerals only; no Mohs scale.
items.misconceptions: Scratch test confused with streak test or luster.

items.stem: Agent Elena observes a sample of the mineral calcite and writes down four notes in her notebook. Which note describes the hardness of the calcite sample?
options: The sample looks pale yellow in the classroom light.
The outside of the sample has a glassy shine.
A copper penny can scratch the surface of the sample.
The sample leaves a white line of powder on a tile.
why: Pale yellow tells what color the mineral is, not its scratch hardness.
A glassy shine describes luster, showing how light bounces off the rock.
Spot on! Getting scratched by a penny tests the mineral's hardness.
Leaving colored powder on a tile describes streak rather than hardness.
items.alt: A sample of calcite on a white test plate with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Distinguishing hardness (scratched by a penny) from color, luster, and streak using calcite; allowed minerals only; no Mohs scale numbers; no identifying an unknown mineral.
items.misconceptions: Confusing hardness with luster, color, or streak.

items.stem: Agent Rosa examines a shiny sample of the mineral mica. When she pulls gently at the edge, the mica splits cleanly along flat surfaces into thin sheets. Which physical property of mica is she observing?
why: Streak is the powder color left behind when a mineral rubs across a tile.
Hardness tests how easily a mineral's surface scratches with a tool.
Color is the shade of light a mineral reflects, not how it splits.
Spot on! Cleavage is the property of a mineral splitting cleanly along flat surfaces.
items.alt: A sample of mica splitting into flat, thin sheets on the left.
items.tisCheck: Cleavage defined and identified using mica splitting into thin flat sheets; allowed minerals only; no identifying an unknown mineral.
items.misconceptions: Confusing cleavage (splitting along flat surfaces) with hardness, color, or streak.

items.stem: Graphite is a soft mineral used in pencil lead. When a student rubs a piece of graphite across a rough white tile, it leaves a dark gray line of powder. Which property of graphite is the student testing?
why: Streak color is the color of the powder a mineral leaves when rubbed on a white tile.
Cleavage is how a mineral breaks along flat surfaces, not the powder it leaves behind.
Luster is how shiny or dull a mineral's surface looks in the light.
Hardness is tested by seeing what can scratch a mineral, not by the color of its powder.
items.alt: A piece of graphite dragged across a white tile, leaving a dark gray line of powder, with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Graphite streak color tested on a white tile; allowed minerals only; no identifying an unknown mineral.
items.misconceptions: Confusing streak color with cleavage, luster, or hardness.

items.stem: Marcus tests a sample of the mineral pyrite. It has a bright shine like polished metal. When he rubs it on a rough white tile, it leaves a greenish black line of powder. Which two properties of pyrite did Marcus observe?
why: He did not scratch the mineral or split it along flat surfaces.
The shiny metal-like surface is luster, and the line of powder on the tile is streak.
Neither cleavage nor mass was tested in this observation.
Looking through the mineral was not part of his test.
items.alt: A shiny pyrite sample dragged across a white tile, leaving a greenish black line of powder, with a hand lens nearby.
items.tisCheck: Pyrite properties (metallic luster and greenish black streak); allowed minerals only; no identifying an unknown mineral.
items.misconceptions: Confusing luster with streak or hardness.

items.stem: Agent Kai spots a live oak tree growing near a limestone boulder. Over many years, a root grows into a crack and pushes until the rock splits apart. What is this an example of?
why: Erosion carries rock pieces away, but these broken chunks stayed in place.
Tree roots do not make extreme heat to melt rock.
No freezing ice was involved in this tree root test.
Spot on! The growing root cracked the rock in place, which is weathering.
items.alt: A cliff with a crack, a tree root splitting the rock, and a stream carrying pebbles downhill.
items.tisCheck: Physical weathering by plants; no landforms assessed; no dissolving of limestone.
items.misconceptions: Weathering and erosion used as the same word.

items.stem: Agent Maya monitors a creek near Tallahassee after heavy rain. The fast water carries sand and pebbles downstream to a new place. Which process is the creek showing?
options: weathering, because the rocks are breaking into pieces
erosion, because the water is moving sand and pebbles to a new place
weathering, because the water turns brown
erosion, because the rocks are melting in the water
why: Nothing in the creek report says the rocks broke apart, only that water carried them.
Spot on! Erosion happens when rushing water or wind carries rock pieces to a new place.
Brown water shows mud moving along the creek, which is erosion rather than weathering.
Solid rocks do not melt in cold creek water.
items.alt: A cliff with a crack, a tree root splitting the rock, and a stream carrying pebbles downhill.
items.tisCheck: Erosion by water vs weathering; no landforms named or assessed.
items.misconceptions: Any change to rock called weathering; erosion thought to need breaking.

items.stem: Agent Leo visits a mine in central Florida that digs a resource out of the ground. Farmers use it to make fertilizer that helps crops grow. Which Florida resource is it?
why: Solar energy comes from bright sunlight, not from underground mines.
Wind is moving air in the sky that cannot be dug out of the ground.
Spot on! Phosphate is mined in central Florida and used to make crop fertilizer.
Limestone is mined for road building and concrete, not crop fertilizer.
items.alt: A Florida outline with small icons for a water well, a quarry, a wind turbine, and a solar panel.
items.tisCheck: Florida resources limited to water, phosphate, oil, limestone, silicon, wind and solar energy (SC.4.E.6.6).
items.misconceptions: Phosphate and limestone confused; energy sources thought to be mined.

items.stem: Agent Sam helps a Florida county choose resources that will not run out. Based on the table, which two resources should the county choose?
why: Spot on! Wind and sunlight are renewable resources that naturally return every single day.
Oil and phosphate take millions of years to form, so they are nonrenewable.
Wind is renewable, but oil takes millions of years to form.
Sunlight is renewable, but phosphate deposits take millions of years to build.

visual.title: Where Resources Come From
columns: How it is made or replaced
rows: Formed from the remains of living things over millions of years
Built up in rock layers over millions of years
Moves every day as the Sun heats the air

items.alt: A table: oil formed over millions of years, phosphate built up over millions of years, wind moves every day, and sunlight reaches Florida every day.
items.tisCheck: Renewable vs nonrenewable (SC.4.E.6.3) with the allowed Florida resources; no computation.
items.misconceptions: Resources found in Florida thought to last forever; every natural resource thought to be renewable.

items.stem: A park ranger lists four changes she saw on a field trip. Which change is erosion and not weathering?
options: A root splits a boulder in two.
Wind carries sand across a beach and piles it into a dune.
Water freezes in a crack and breaks the rock.
A rock cracks after many hot days and cold nights.
why: A root that breaks rock is weathering by plants.
The wind moves sand to a new place, which is erosion.
Ice that breaks rock in a crack is weathering.
Heating and cooling that cracks rock is weathering.
items.alt: A cliff with a crack, a tree root splitting the rock, and a stream carrying pebbles downhill.
items.tisCheck: Weathering by plants, ice and temperature change vs erosion by wind; the dune is context and no landform is assessed.
items.misconceptions: Wind thought to only weather rock; erosion and weathering mixed up.

items.stem: Water freezes in a crack in a boulder high on a mountain, and a piece breaks off. Later, the piece falls into a river. The river carries it far downstream. Which list names the two processes in order?
why: This reverses the order, since the rock broke before it was carried.
Being carried by the river is moving, not breaking.
Ice breaking the rock is breaking, not moving.
Ice broke the rock first, which is weathering, and then the river moved the piece, which is erosion.
items.alt: A cliff with a crack, a tree root splitting the rock, and a stream carrying pebbles downhill.
items.tisCheck: Weathering by ice, then erosion by gravity and water, in one story; no landforms assessed.
items.misconceptions: The order of weathering and erosion reversed; one word used for both.

items.stem: Agent Rosa surveys the Florida coast after a storm. Large ocean waves carry tons of sand away from the beach to a new place. What is this process of moving sand called?
why: Spot on! Waves carrying sand to a new location is an example of erosion.
Weathering breaks rock down where it sits without carrying the sand away.
Cementation is the gluing of sediment grains together into sedimentary rock.
Melting turns rock into liquid magma with scorching heat.
items.alt: A slope where moving water carries sand and pebbles away to a new place.
items.tisCheck: Erosion by water moving sand vs physical weathering (SC.4.E.6.4); Florida beach context.
items.misconceptions: Confusing weathering (breaking) with erosion (moving).

items.stem: After a heavy rain in central Florida, loose soil and broken pieces of limestone slide down the steep side of a sinkhole to the bottom. Which statement best explains this change?
options: Weathering happened, because gravity broke large boulders into sand.
Erosion happened, because gravity moved the soil and rock pieces to a new place.
Weathering happened, because the rain broke the soil into smaller bits without moving it.
Erosion happened, because tree roots grew into cracks and split the rock in place.
why: Weathering breaks rock in place, while sliding downhill is movement to a new place.
Erosion is the movement of rock and soil from one place to another by gravity, water, wind, or ice.
The soil and rock pieces moved to the bottom of the sinkhole, so this is erosion, not weathering in place.
Tree roots splitting rock in place is physical weathering, not erosion.
items.alt: A steep rocky slope with loose rock falling downhill and water carrying pebbles at the bottom.
items.tisCheck: Erosion by gravity moving loose limestone and soil down a slope vs physical weathering (SC.4.E.6.4); no chemical weathering or dissolving.
items.misconceptions: Confusing erosion by gravity with physical weathering in place.

items.stem: Water seeps into a small crack in a boulder during winter. When the water freezes into ice, it takes up more space and splits the boulder into two pieces that stay in place. Which statement describes this change?
options: It is erosion, because wind carried the boulder down a hill.
It is erosion, because gravity pulled the boulder into a river.
It is weathering, because freezing water expanded and broke the rock.
It is melting, because ice turned the solid rock into liquid.
why: Wind moving rock is erosion, and this boulder was broken by ice where it sat.
Gravity moving rock to a new place is erosion, not ice splitting a rock in place.
When water freezes into ice, it expands and breaks rock apart in place, which is physical weathering.
Ice splits the solid rock physically rather than melting it into liquid.
items.alt: A rocky cliff with a crack labeled Ice in crack where rock is splitting apart.
items.tisCheck: Physical weathering by freezing water expanding in a crack (SC.4.E.6.4); breaking without moving.
items.misconceptions: Confusing ice wedging (physical weathering) with erosion; thinking water shrinks when it freezes.

items.stem: A scientist compares changes to rock and soil around a Florida river basin. Which event is an example of weathering rather than erosion?
options: Mud sliding down a river bank into rushing water.
River water sweeping pebbles downstream to the ocean.
Wind blowing loose dirt across a cleared farm field.
Tree roots cracking a limestone ledge into small pieces.
why: Mud sliding into water is erosion because gravity moves the soil.
Moving pebbles downstream is erosion because the pebbles change location.
Wind carrying dirt away to another area is erosion.
Tree roots splitting limestone breaks the rock apart where it sits, which is physical weathering.
items.alt: A cliff with a crack, a tree root splitting the rock, and a stream carrying pebbles downhill.
items.tisCheck: Distinguishing physical weathering by plants (breaking rock in place) from erosion (moving rock and soil).
items.misconceptions: Thinking plant roots move rock to new places rather than breaking it in place.

items.stem: A class studies resources found in Florida and sorts them into renewable resources and nonrenewable resources. Which natural resource found in Florida is nonrenewable?
options: phosphate rock mined from the ground
why: Fresh water is a renewable resource that is replaced by rain in the water cycle.
Sunlight is a renewable resource that shines every day and cannot be used up.
Phosphate rock formed millions of years ago and cannot be replaced once mined, so it is nonrenewable.
Wind is a renewable resource that is replaced naturally every day.
items.alt: A Florida outline with icons for a water well, a phosphate mine, a wind turbine, and a solar panel.
items.tisCheck: Renewable vs nonrenewable Florida resources (SC.4.E.6.3, SC.4.E.6.6); allowed Florida resources list only.
items.misconceptions: Confusing mined mineral resources with renewable natural cycles.

items.stem: Strong winds along a Florida barrier island pick up loose sand grains and carry them across the shore to build sand dunes. Which statement correctly identifies what the wind is doing?
options: The wind is causing weathering by moving whole sand grains to a new spot.
The wind is changing the sand grains into metamorphic rock.
The wind is melting the sand grains into liquid rock.
The wind is causing erosion by moving sand from one place to another.
why: Moving sand from one place to another is erosion, while weathering is breaking rock into smaller pieces.
Wind does not apply high heat or deep pressure to form metamorphic rock.
Wind on a beach does not melt sand grains.
Wind picking up sand and carrying it to a new place is an example of erosion.

visual.title: Beach notes
rows: Loose, dry sand lies on the flat beach.
Strong wind blows sand grains across the beach.
A new pile of sand has formed behind the beach.

items.alt: A table shows loose, dry sand in the morning, wind blowing sand in the afternoon, and a new pile of sand the next day.
items.tisCheck: Erosion by wind vs physical weathering (SC.4.E.6.4); dunes used as Florida coastal context, no landform assessed. A beach observation table replaced the mismatched cliff, root, and stream diagram.
items.misconceptions: Confusing wind erosion (moving sand) with weathering (breaking rock).

codex.title: Plant roots
codex.line: A root that grows into a crack can split rock apart, which is weathering.

codex.title: Ice in cracks
codex.line: Water that freezes in a crack takes up more space and can split the rock.

codex.title: Glaciers
codex.line: A glacier is a huge sheet of ice that moves slowly downhill and carries rock along, which is erosion.
